50	
51	**Summary:** Completed Section 3 of the add-harnaas-foundation change — help groups, the explicit-attachment rule, the local --json flag helper and the stdout/stderr output contract — taking the change from 17/74 to 22/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.

54	- cmd/harnaas/cli/root.go declares the root's help groups (setup, then assets) in display order, and adds addCommand(parent, child, groupID) as the single way a command joins the tree: it declares the group on first use, sets the child's GroupID, and panics naming command and group on an unknown id — surfacing a wiring typo at construction instead of cobra's execute-time panic

57	- cmd/harnaas/cli/output.go states the output contract in one place and implements it: printJSON writes the document to cmd.OutOrStdout() indented, with HTML escaping off so an ampersand in a source ref survives verbatim, and newline-terminated; advisef sends progress and warning text to cmd.ErrOrStderr()
58	- cmd/harnaas/cli/root_test.go covers section 3.5 and 3.2: the root declares no persistent flags and a subcommand inherits nothing; --json is accepted only on the command that declares it and fails as 'unknown flag: --json' on a sibling and on the root; groups are declared in display order and none is declared empty; addCommand rejects an unknown group; and an AST pass over non-test sources asserts the package declares no init, so the no-self-registration rule survives a gochecknoinits suppression

63	- Cobra renders a help header for every declared group whether or not it has members — verified with a scratch test showing a bare 'Empty Commands:' line. That is why helpGroups is a declaration list and addCommand declares a group only on first use: eager declaration would show empty headings for install and lint until their own changes land. The cost is that group display order equals command attachment order, which TestHelpGroupsAreDeclaredInDisplayOrder pins.
64	- Cobra's checkCommandGroups panics at execute time for a command whose GroupID names an undeclared group, but AddCommand itself does no checking — so a group declared after the commands that use it is a latent panic, not a compile error.
65	- Section 3.5's 'wrong positional-argument count prints the subcommand's usage' and 'an unrecognized subcommand exits non-zero' were already covered by iteration 2's main_test.go (TestReportErrorShowsTheDeepestSubcommandUsageForAnArgCountError and TestErrorSwitchClassifiesRealCobraErrors); only the persistent-flag and unknown---json assertions were still missing.

71	### Iteration 4
72	
73	**Summary:** Added the paths and logging foundation packages (tasks 4.2 and 4.3) and wired both into the entrypoint, taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 22/74 to 24/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
74	
75	**Changes:**
76	- cmd/harnaas/cli/paths resolves the project root by walking up for a .git marker — accepting the file form git writes in a worktree or submodule, and letting the nearest enclosing repository win as git itself does — through a pure Resolve(startDir) that takes a directory rather than reading one
77	- paths.WithDiscoveredRoot is the single sanctioned reader of the process working directory, carrying the resolved root or the failure in the context; the forbidigo suppression lives there, inside the abstraction the ban's message names
78	- paths.ProjectRoot(ctx) surfaces the discovery failure at the moment a command asks for a root, so --version, --help and an unknown-command diagnostic keep working outside a repository; a context that never established a root reports ErrRootNotEstablished as a wiring failure distinct from the user-facing *NoProjectRootError
79	- *NoProjectRootError is typed so a command can recognise the condition without matching message text, and renders as problem-then-fix: which directory was searched, then to run harnaas inside a repository or create one with git init
80	- cmd/harnaas/cli/logging writes structured slog records to a file under the user's cache directory (HARNAAS_LOG_FILE overrides it, HARNAAS_LOG_LEVEL sets the threshold, both documented at their only read site), never to a terminal stream
81	- logging discards records where the log file cannot be opened, rather than the reference CLI's fallback to stderr, and Open returns no error because there is nowhere to report one to — a warning on the terminal is the interleaving the log file exists to prevent
82	- logging.WithCommand and logging.WithComponent label every record with the command the user ran and the subsystem that produced it, ahead of the call site's own attributes; the API takes slog.Attr only, so every logged value arrives as a named field
83	- The package doc states the privacy rule as a hard rule with harnaas's own reason: the files it handles are a team's instructions and rules, exactly the content nobody expects to find copied into a log they did not know existed
84	- main.go establishes the project root and opens the log before executing the command tree, and records the run's outcome by exit code and error *type* — never the error message, because errors from later phases will quote the manifest that produced them
85	- Test coverage: resolution from a nested directory matching resolution from the root, the marker-file form, the nearest-repository rule, the outside-a-repository diagnostic naming directory and fix, context carrying and key isolation, plus logging tests that redirect stdout, stderr and slog's default logger and assert on cleanup that nothing reached any of them
86	- CLAUDE.md's logging section now records the two load-bearing decisions — discard rather than fall back to a stream, and keep the log outside the project — so a later change does not reintroduce either
87	
88	**Learnings:**
89	- Logging cannot live under the project: task 8.11 requires that after init no .harnaas/ directory exists and harnaas.json is the only file that appeared, so the log file must go under os.UserCacheDir. Task 9.5's 'redirect home, cache and config under t.TempDir' harness confirms per-user state is where harnaas keeps everything that is not the manifest.
90	- The reference CLI's logging falls back to stderr when the log file cannot be opened; copying that would corrupt a --json document, so harnaas discards instead. The uninitialised logger must also be a discarding logger rather than slog.Default(), which writes to stderr — a stray log call before Open would otherwise print.
91	- sloglint's attr-only: true is already configured in .golangci.yaml, which is the mechanical half of task 4.3's 'attribute-only API'; taking ...slog.Attr in the wrapper signatures makes it a compile-time guarantee at harnaas's own call sites too.
92	- staticcheck ST1005 rejects an errors.New string ending in punctuation or a newline, which rules out the problem-blank-line-fix diagnostic shape for a sentinel error. Giving the sentinel a small unexported type with an Error() method keeps errors.Is working and keeps the message shaped like every other diagnostic.
93	- sloglint also rejects slog.NewJSONHandler(io.Discard, ...) in favour of Go 1.24's slog.DiscardHandler, and gocritic's mapKey flags a table-test map key with leading or trailing whitespace — a case worth testing, so that table has to be a slice of structs.
94	- t.Chdir forbids t.Parallel, which is the practical argument for making root resolution a pure function over a directory: only the one test that exercises WithDiscoveredRoot has to move the process, and every other paths test runs in parallel.
95	- t.TempDir sits under a symlink on macOS (/var → /private/var), so a root discovered through the working directory comes back spelled differently from the path the test created; the paths tests resolve symlinks in their scratch-directory helper rather than teaching the package to rewrite paths.
96	- errcheck's check-blank: true makes `_ = f()` on an error a lint failure, so a deliberately-ignored error needs a real branch or a signature that returns no error at all — which pushed logging.Open to return only its closer, with the unexported open(path) keeping the failure visible to tests.
97	
98	### Iteration 5
99	
100	**Summary:** Added the palette and jsonutil foundation packages (tasks 4.4 and 4.6) and routed the --json output path through jsonutil's canonical encoder, taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 24/74 to 26/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
101	
102	**Changes:**
103	- cmd/harnaas/cli/palette is a zero-dependency package of base16 ANSI slot constants held as plain strings, so harnaas's colours are a request the terminal answers with the user's own theme rather than a hex value that is only correct on the machine it was picked on
104	- palette's semantic aliases (Accent, Accent2, Muted, Success, Error, Warning, Info) are what styles declare against, with the raw slot names reserved for colour that carries no meaning; the package documents that one Muted slot rather than a range of greys is what keeps de-emphasis reading as one level
105	- palette deliberately declares no body-text alias, and the package comment states why: body text stays unstyled so it renders in the terminal's default foreground and inverts with the background, where pinning White would erase every line on a light terminal
106	- palette's tests read the package's own source via AST so a colour added later is covered without anyone remembering to extend the test, assert every declared colour is a slot in 0..15, assert no alias name reads as body text, and assert no two semantic aliases collapse onto the same slot
107	- cmd/harnaas/cli/jsonutil.Marshal is harnaas's single JSON document format — two-space indent, HTML left unescaped so an ampersand in a source ref survives, and exactly one trailing newline — with the indent a constant rather than a parameter because the whole point is that a manifest and a --json document are not formatted differently for want of a shared default
108	- jsonutil.WriteFileAtomic stages the bytes in a sibling file in the destination directory, flushes them to disk, applies the permission and renames over the destination, so a reader sees either the whole old file or the whole new one; staging beside the destination is what keeps the rename a rename rather than a cross-filesystem copy
109	- WriteFileAtomic removes the staging file unconditionally via defer on both success and failure, and flushes the destination directory best-effort after the rename so a crash cannot leave new contents on disk behind a directory entry still pointing at the old file
110	- WriteFileAtomic delegates to an unexported writeFileAtomic taking the flush step as a parameter, giving the failure-path guarantee a test seam without a mutable global, so the injected-failure tests still run in parallel
111	- jsonutil tests cover the format line by line (indentation is what is under test), HTML characters left verbatim, the single trailing newline, a round trip, an unencodable value returning no partial document, file creation and full replacement of a longer previous file, permission application, an unusable destination directory, and the two injected-failure cases — previous file intact and nothing created — each asserting on the directory's entries so no staging file can survive under a name the test would have to guess
112	- printJSON in cmd/harnaas/cli/output.go now encodes through jsonutil.Marshal and writes the finished bytes, so the --json document and the manifest init will write share one definition of the format, and an unencodable value returns an error with stdout still empty instead of a half-streamed document ahead of the entrypoint's error message
113	- Tasks 4.4 and 4.6 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md; 4.7 left unchecked because its accessible-mode and piped-stream clauses depend on 4.5's uiform and interactive packages
114	
115	**Learnings:**
116	- golangci-lint's std-error-handling exclusion preset already covers os.Remove and *.Close, so `_ = os.Remove(...)` and a deferred Close stay clean even with errcheck's check-blank: true — but Sync is not on that list, so the best-effort directory flush still needs an explicit nolint with a reason. This is the boundary that decides which dropped errors need a suppression and which do not.
117	- testifylint's encoded-compare rule rejects asserting an exact JSON string with assert.Equal and pushes toward assert.JSONEq, which would defeat a test whose whole subject is indentation and trailing newline. Splitting the document on newlines and comparing the resulting []string satisfies the linter and reads better, because a failure names the line that moved.
118	- Injecting a mid-write failure portably needs a seam: making the rename fail is platform-specific (POSIX rename over a regular file succeeds), so passing the flush step as a function parameter to an unexported implementation is the way to exercise the failure path on both Windows and POSIX. Unlike a package-level var it does not force the test to give up t.Parallel.
119	- On Windows the staging file must be closed before the deferred os.Remove can delete it, so the write/flush/close sequence has to close on every path including the ones where write or flush failed — otherwise the 'no staging file survives' guarantee holds on POSIX and silently fails on Windows.
120	- os.Chmod on Windows only toggles a read-only bit rather than storing the requested mode, so the permission assertion has to skip there; the file-contents and no-litter assertions still run on every platform.
121	- The `check` mise task fans out fmt, lint:go, lint:gofmt, lint:gomod, lint:mise and lint:shellcheck but not lint:licenses — that gate is a separate task, so a change adding dependencies has to run it explicitly.
122	
123	### Iteration 6
124	
125	**Summary:** Added the interactive and uiform foundation packages (tasks 4.5 and 4.7), completing Section 4 of the add-harnaas-foundation change and taking it from 26/74 to 28/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
126	
127	**Changes:**
128	- cmd/harnaas/cli/interactive resolves whether harnaas may prompt from the command's own streams plus the environment — HARNAAS_TEST_TTY override, then go test, then coding-agent sentinels (CLAUDECODE, CURSOR_AGENT, GEMINI_CLI, COPILOT_CLI, PI_CODING_AGENT), then CI, then both streams being terminals — with the decision biased towards 'no' because a flag-driven path always exists while a prompt shown to something that cannot answer hangs rather than degrades
129	- interactive deliberately tests the attached streams rather than probing a controlling terminal, which keeps the question answerable on Windows and keeps it honest under redirection: `harnaas init > out.txt` has a terminal attached to the process and still must not prompt
130	- interactive.ShouldStyle is the single gate in front of the palette, honouring NO_COLOR and excluding TERM=cygwin, and is kept a separate question from CanPrompt because a run inside a coding agent must not be prompted and may still be styled
131	- Both decisions are split into pure cores (canPrompt, shouldStyle) taking getenv and the terminal answer as parameters, because `go test` can never present a real terminal and the exported functions would short-circuit before the environment gates were reached
132	- cmd/harnaas/cli/uiform is the only place harnaas builds a form, so accessible mode and the base16 theme are applied without anyone having to remember them; New takes explicit streams so prompts render on stderr and cannot corrupt a --json document on stdout
133	- uiform.Theme unsets the pinned foreground on titles and unselected options in both the focused and blurred variants so they inherit the terminal's default text colour, and points selection at palette.Accent — the theme declares no colour of its own
134	- uiform.Confirm returns ErrCancelled for a dismissed prompt rather than folding cancellation into a 'no', because the init spec requires a cancelled prompt to write nothing and exit non-zero while a decline is an ordinary answer
135	- uiform.Confirm consults the context directly before and after running the form, because huh reports a cancelled context as ErrTimeout and ignores the context entirely in accessible mode
136	- Test coverage: a table over every prompting gate including piped streams and the CI=false escape hatch, each agent sentinel individually, real os.Pipe and bytes.Buffer both answering 'not a terminal', the styling gates, accessible mode completing a prompt against non-terminal streams, cancellation reported separately from declining, and the theme's unstyled-titles and accent-selection guarantees
137	- charm.land/huh/v2, charm.land/lipgloss/v2 and golang.org/x/term added to go.mod, with the go-licenses gate confirming all 20 new transitive dependencies are on the allowlist
138	- CLAUDE.md's non-interactive completeness section now records the two load-bearing decisions — prompting resolved from streams rather than a controlling terminal, and a cancelled prompt distinct from a 'no' — so a later change does not reintroduce either
139	- Tasks 4.5 and 4.7 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md, completing Section 4
140	
141	**Learnings:**
142	- huh v2 reports a cancelled context as huh.ErrTimeout, not ErrUserAborted or context.Canceled — its run() maps tea.ErrProgramKilled to ErrTimeout because a timeout is the only reason it cancels a context itself. Matching on huh's error alone silently misclassifies a signal-driven cancellation; consulting ctx.Err() is the only reliable test.
143	- huh's accessible path (runAccessible) ignores the context entirely and runs synchronously against the given reader/writer, so a cancellation arriving mid-question is invisible until the prompt returns. Any wrapper that must honour cancellation has to check the context after the run as well as before it.
144	- Accessible mode is what makes a prompt testable at all: the full-screen path needs a terminal to redraw, while runAccessible works against a strings.Reader and a bytes.Buffer. A test that sets ACCESSIBLE and completes a prompt on non-terminal streams is therefore a genuine assertion that accessible mode was honoured, not a proxy for one.
145	- huh's accessible PromptString breaks out of its re-prompt loop on EOF rather than looping forever, and an empty line falls through to the default — so a test can feed a bare reader without hanging.
146	- The reference CLI's /dev/tty probe plus raw-mode ioctl is POSIX-only and would need three build-tagged files that do nothing on Windows. Testing the command's own streams for terminal-ness covers the same cases portably and additionally catches redirection, which the /dev/tty probe misses.
147	- lint:gomod necessarily fails in any iteration that adds a dependency, because it runs `go mod tidy` and then asserts `git status --porcelain go.mod go.sum` is empty — uncommitted additions are indistinguishable from an untidy tree. The signal to check is that `go mod tidy` produced no *further* change beyond the intended one.
148	- golangci-lint accepted the whole huh/lipgloss surface without a single suppression beyond the two gosec G115 fd conversions, so the charm v2 stack imposes no lint debt on this configuration.
149	
150	### Iteration 7
151	
152	**Summary:** Added the data-only harness roster package (Section 5, tasks 5.1–5.4), taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 28/74 to 32/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
153	
154	**Changes:**
155	- cmd/harnaas/cli/harness declares the Harness descriptor — canonical ID (a named string type so a source key or display name cannot be passed as a harness), display name, PerUserLocation, and ProjectEvidence — with claude-code as the only roster entry and Default pointing at it
156	- Project evidence is held as project-root-relative paths ('.claude', 'CLAUDE.md') rather than a predicate, so init does the stat calls and the roster holds no behaviour the install adapters could later disagree with
157	- Lookup helpers: IDs() and All() returning deep copies in the roster's sorted order, Lookup, Recognized, and HasPerUserLocation as the query manifest scope validation calls
158	- *UnknownError carries the id exactly as written plus the recognized list, and renders problem-then-fix so a caller can attribute the failure to an asset entry without matching message text; HasPerUserLocation returns that error for an unknown id rather than false, because a typo and an unsupported scope need different edits
159	- Tests cover the default being itself recognized, sorted and call-stable ordering, the unknown-id message naming the input and listing alternatives identically on every run, every entry being usable with relative non-escaping evidence, and callers being unable to mutate the roster through All() or IDs()
160	- Two AST guardrails over non-test sources: the package imports no filesystem, network or environment package (encoding 'data only, no write behaviour'), and declares no package init so the roster stays a readable literal
161	- CLAUDE.md records the two load-bearing decisions — the roster is data only with the caller doing I/O, and an unrecognized id is an error because the harnesses list states a guarantee rather than exclusivity
162	- Tasks 5.1 through 5.4 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md

1	## Purpose
2	
3	Defines `harnaas.json`, the committed, hand-edited file in which a project declares which harness
4	assets it wants and where they come from. It covers the file's location, its strict decoding, the
5	document shape, the `sources` block, how each asset's type and id are inferred from its path, target
6	and scope defaulting, and the validation that must pass before any later phase reads it.
7	
8	## ADDED Requirements
9	
10	### Requirement: Manifest Location And Root-Only Rule
11	
12	The manifest SHALL be a single file named `harnaas.json` at the repository root, resolved from the
13	project root carried in the request context so it is found from any subdirectory. A `harnaas.json`
14	discovered in a subdirectory of the project SHALL be a validation error naming the root manifest as
15	the only one harnaas reads. When the root has no manifest, a command requiring one SHALL say so and
16	name `harnaas init`.
17	
18	#### Scenario: Manifest found from a subdirectory
19	
20	- **WHEN** a command runs in a nested directory of a project whose root contains `harnaas.json`
21	- **THEN** that manifest is loaded and its relative paths resolve against the project root
22	
23	#### Scenario: Manifest in a subdirectory is an error
24	
25	- **WHEN** a `harnaas.json` exists in a subdirectory of the project
26	- **THEN** the run fails naming that file and stating that only the manifest at the repository root
27	  is read
28	
29	#### Scenario: Missing manifest is reported actionably
30	
31	- **WHEN** a command requiring the manifest runs in a project with no root `harnaas.json`
32	- **THEN** the CLI reports that no manifest was found, names `harnaas init` as the way to create one,
33	  and exits non-zero
34	
35	### Requirement: Manifest Is Never Written By harnaas
36	
37	Apart from `harnaas init` creating the file once, harnaas SHALL never write, rewrite, reformat or
38	normalize `harnaas.json`. `install` and `lint` SHALL treat it as read-only input: adding, removing or
39	repinning an asset is a hand edit. Every remedy harnaas reports for a manifest problem MUST be
40	phrased as an edit for a person to make, never as a command that edits the file.
41	
42	#### Scenario: Install leaves the manifest untouched
43	
44	- **WHEN** `harnaas install` runs against any manifest, including one it reports problems with
45	- **THEN** `harnaas.json` is byte-identical afterwards
46	
47	#### Scenario: Remedy is an edit, not a write
48	
49	- **WHEN** a command reports that an asset entry needs to change
50	- **THEN** the remedy states the exact edit to make in `harnaas.json` and no command that would apply
51	  it automatically is offered
52	
53	### Requirement: Strict Manifest Decoding
54	
55	Because the manifest is committed and hand-edited, decoding SHALL reject unknown fields and malformed
56	JSON, naming the offending field or the parse location. A decoding failure MUST NOT fall back to
57	partial or default values and MUST leave every asset in the document unprocessed.
58	
59	#### Scenario: Misspelled field is rejected
60	
61	- **WHEN** the manifest contains a top-level key spelled `assests` instead of `assets`
62	- **THEN** loading fails naming the unknown field, and no asset is processed
63	
64	#### Scenario: Malformed JSON is rejected
65	
66	- **WHEN** the manifest is not well-formed JSON
67	- **THEN** loading fails with a parse error identifying the location, and no partial manifest is used
68	
69	### Requirement: Manifest Document Shape
70	
71	The manifest SHALL be a JSON object carrying an integer `version`, a `harnesses` array naming the
72	harnesses assets target by default, a `sources` object mapping a source key to a repository and ref,
73	and an `assets` array whose entries are source strings or override objects. A field whose value has
74	the wrong shape SHALL be rejected naming that field.
75	
76	#### Scenario: Minimal manifest loads
77	
78	- **WHEN** a manifest declares version `1`, harnesses `["claude-code"]`, one source key, and an
79	  `assets` array of source strings
80	- **THEN** it loads successfully and its assets are available to later phases
81	
82	#### Scenario: Assets must be an array
83	
84	- **WHEN** `assets` is present but is not an array
85	- **THEN** loading fails with an error naming the `assets` field
86	
87	### Requirement: Declared Sources Block
88	
89	Every repository and ref SHALL be declared once in `sources` under a short key, and assets SHALL
90	reference that key rather than repeating a repository or ref. A source value SHALL name its kind,
91	repository and ref, as in `github:acme/assets@v1.2.0`. An asset referencing an undeclared key MUST
92	fail naming the key and the `sources` block, and an unrecognized source kind MUST fail naming it.
93	
94	#### Scenario: Several assets share one declared source
95	
96	- **WHEN** two asset strings both begin with the key `acme:` declared as
97	  `github:acme/assets@v1.2.0`
98	- **THEN** both assets resolve against that one repository and ref, declared in exactly one place
99	
100	#### Scenario: Undeclared source key is rejected
101	
102	- **WHEN** an asset string uses a key that `sources` does not declare
103	- **THEN** loading fails naming the key and pointing at the `sources` block
104	
105	#### Scenario: Unrecognized source kind is rejected
106	
107	- **WHEN** a `sources` entry names a kind other than `github` or `local`
108	- **THEN** loading fails naming the unsupported kind and the source key
109	
110	### Requirement: Asset Source String Grammar
111	
112	An asset entry given as a string SHALL take one of two forms: `<sourceKey>:<path>`, where the key is
113	declared in `sources` and the path is relative to that source's root; or a project-local path
114	beginning with `.harnaas/`. A string in neither form — an unprefixed relative path, an absolute path,
115	or a URL — MUST be rejected, naming the entry and both accepted forms.
116	
117	#### Scenario: Keyed remote form is accepted
118	
119	- **WHEN** an asset string is `acme:skills/review` and `acme` is declared in `sources`
120	- **THEN** it resolves to the path `skills/review` within that source
121	
122	#### Scenario: Local form is accepted
123	
124	- **WHEN** an asset string is `.harnaas/rules/house-style.md`
125	- **THEN** it resolves to that path beneath the project's `.harnaas` directory
126	
127	#### Scenario: Unprefixed path is rejected
128	
129	- **WHEN** an asset string is `skills/review` with no source key and no `.harnaas/` prefix
130	- **THEN** loading fails naming the entry and stating both accepted forms
131	
132	### Requirement: Local Source Containment Under .harnaas
133	
134	A local asset path SHALL be relative to the project root and SHALL resolve inside `.harnaas`. A path
135	that is absolute, or that escapes `.harnaas` by traversing upward with parent-directory segments,
136	MUST be rejected at load time reporting that local assets live under `.harnaas`, and its content MUST
137	NOT be read.
138	
139	#### Scenario: Upward traversal is rejected
140	
141	- **WHEN** a local asset path escapes `.harnaas` using parent-directory segments
142	- **THEN** loading fails reporting that local assets must live under `.harnaas`
143	
144	#### Scenario: Absolute local path is rejected
145	
146	- **WHEN** a local asset entry names an absolute filesystem path
147	- **THEN** loading fails reporting that local asset paths must be relative to the project root
148	
149	### Requirement: Type And Id Inferred From The Asset Path
150	
151	An asset's type and id SHALL be inferred from its path: the containing directory names the type —
152	`skills/` → skill, `rules/` → rule, `instructions/` → instruction, `commands/` → command, `agents/` →
153	persona — and the leaf names the id, with any file extension removed. A path whose containing
154	directory is none of those names MUST be rejected, naming the entry and directing the author to the
155	object form.
156	
157	#### Scenario: Skill inferred from a keyed path
158	
159	- **WHEN** an asset string is `acme:skills/review`
160	- **THEN** the asset has type `skill` and id `review`
161	
162	#### Scenario: Persona inferred from an agents directory
163	
164	- **WHEN** an asset string is `acme:agents/reviewer`
165	- **THEN** the asset has type `persona` and id `reviewer`
166	
167	#### Scenario: Extension stripped from a local file asset
168	
169	- **WHEN** an asset string is `.harnaas/instructions/tone.md`
170	- **THEN** the asset has type `instruction` and id `tone`
171	
172	#### Scenario: Unrecognized containing directory is rejected
173	
174	- **WHEN** an asset string is `acme:prompts/review`, whose containing directory names no type
175	- **THEN** loading fails naming the entry and stating that the object form must declare the type
176	
177	### Requirement: Asset Object Override Form
178	
179	An asset entry given as an object SHALL carry its source string plus any of `type`, `id`, `targets`
180	and `scope`, each overriding what the path would otherwise imply or the manifest would otherwise
181	default to. The object form SHALL be the only way to state a per-asset type, id, target list or
182	scope, and it MUST be decoded as strictly as the rest of the document.
183	
184	#### Scenario: Object supplies type and id for an unconventional layout
185	
186	- **WHEN** an asset object names a source path whose directory does not follow the convention and
187	  declares `type` and `id` explicitly

It is specified here, in the foundation, rather than in `add-harnaas-lint` for two reasons: the
contract belongs to the process, not to one command; and reserving it up front lets this change also
state the negative rule — that no other command may ever exit `2` — which is not enforceable if the
code is introduced later by the command that uses it.

### Signals are re-raised, not swallowed

The first interrupt cancels the root context and prints a notice; a second forces exit. On termination
the process re-raises the original signal to itself instead of calling a plain exit, falling back to
`128`+signum only where re-raising is unsupported. The source CLI explains why this matters: a shell
aborts a `while true; do …; done` loop only when the child is *killed by* the signal. A plain exit with
status 130 is an ordinary exit, so the loop keeps respawning and the user's Ctrl-C never escapes.

### Decoding strictness follows who writes the file, not what the file is called

This is the subtlest imported rule, and it decides the manifest's behaviour. Committed, human-edited
files decode **strictly** — an unknown field is nearly always a typo, and surfacing it immediately is
worth the cost. Machine-rewritten files decode **leniently**, because a newer binary introduces fields
an older binary would then reject, bricking the file for everyone still on the older version, with no
fix available to the user who hits it.

Applying that test rather than a naming convention is what puts harnaas's two files on opposite sides:
`harnaas.json` is hand-edited, so it is strict; `harnaas.lock.json` is machine-written, so it is
lenient. That split is only coherent because ownership is recorded in the lockfile rather than in the
manifest or in markers inside installed files — see
[0001-ownership-lives-in-the-lockfile.md](../../../docs/adr/0001-ownership-lives-in-the-lockfile.md).

### harnaas never writes the manifest, and every remedy is an edit

Apart from `init` creating the file once, no command writes, reformats or normalizes `harnaas.json`.
This is why there is no `add`, `remove` or `update` command: they would exist only to edit a file a
person can edit.

The reason is that the manifest is the artifact a team reviews. A tool that rewrites it makes its diffs
untrustworthy — a reviewer can no longer tell an intentional pin bump from a normalization pass — and
reformatting churn would land in every pull request that ran a command. Phrasing every remedy as an
exact edit rather than a fix command also keeps the human in the loop on the one decision that
actually matters: which version of somebody else's content this repository is about to trust.

### An asset's type and id are inferred from its path, with an object form as the escape hatch

`acme:skills/review` says everything: the containing directory names the type, the leaf names the id.
Writing `{"source": "acme:skills/review", "type": "skill", "id": "review"}` would restate in twelve
tokens what the path already said, and would introduce a second source of truth that can disagree with
the first.

The convention is not invented here — `skills/`, `commands/` and `agents/` are already how asset
repositories are laid out, because that is how the harnesses themselves read them. Inference makes the
common case one string per asset, which keeps the manifest short enough to review as a list. A path
whose containing directory names no type is an error that points at the object form rather than a
guess, so the failure mode is a message rather than an asset silently installed as the wrong type.

The object form then carries the genuinely per-asset decisions that no path can express — a narrowed
`targets` list and a non-default `scope` — so there is exactly one place to look when an asset behaves
differently from its neighbours.

### Sources are declared once under a key, and assets reference the key

A repository and ref appear exactly once, in `sources`. The alternative — a full `github:acme/assets@v1.2.0`
prefix on every asset string — makes a version bump an N-line edit where N is the number of assets from
that repository, and makes it possible for two assets to disagree about which ref they came from while
both look correct in review.

Keying also gives the later changes a natural unit: `install` fetches one archive per repository and
commit regardless of how many assets it covers, and `lint` checks for a newer tag once per source
rather than once per asset. Both fall out of the manifest shape instead of needing a deduplication
pass.

### The `harnesses` list states a guarantee, not exclusivity

Because skills and instructions land in shared locations that many harnesses read — see
[0002-shared-agents-target-before-per-harness.md](../../../docs/adr/0002-shared-agents-target-before-per-harness.md)
— a harness that is *not* in the list will still see assets installed for one that is. The list
therefore means "the harnesses we guarantee this works for", not "the harnesses that can see this".

This matters to the manifest's validation rules, which is why it is settled here: an unrecognized
harness name is an error because it is a guarantee harnaas cannot make, but an asset installed for
`claude-code` being visible to Cursor is not a bug to be prevented. It also sets what `init`'s
detection is for — pre-filling a list of guarantees, not enumerating what is installed on the machine.

### Scope defaults to project, and `user` is validated rather than degraded

`user` scope is accepted only where a target harness has an unambiguous per-user location, and
declaring it elsewhere is a validation error. Silently falling back to project scope would install the
asset somewhere the author did not ask for and would not notice, and a wrong install location is
exactly the failure harnaas exists to eliminate.

An `instruction` is project scope only, and that is a definitional consequence rather than a
limitation: an instruction differs from a rule by surviving a fresh clone inside a committed file —
see
[0003-instruction-content-in-an-agents-md-block.md](../../../docs/adr/0003-instruction-content-in-an-agents-md-block.md).
At user scope there is no clone and no committed file, so the distinction from a rule disappears and
the type would mean nothing.

### One manifest, at the repository root

A `harnaas.json` in a subdirectory is an error naming the root manifest, not a second declaration to
be merged. Merging would make the effective asset set depend on which directory a command ran from,
which contradicts the whole point: the repository declares one set of assets and everyone gets it.
Erroring instead of ignoring is deliberate too — a file named `harnaas.json` that harnaas silently
skips is worse than one it rejects.

### A data-only harness roster ships before the adapters that give it meaning

Manifest validation must reject an unknown harness name and must know whether a harness has an
unambiguous per-user location, and `init` must detect which harnesses a project already uses. All
three needs land in this change, while the adapters that map an asset type to a destination land in
the next one.

The seam is drawn so the two cannot drift into conflict: the roster is **data only** — id, display
name, whether a per-user root exists, and the observable evidence that the harness is present — with
no destination mapping and no write behaviour. `add-harnaas-install` attaches adapters to those ids
and asserts in its registry test that every adapter's id exists in the roster. The alternative,
deferring the roster into `install`, would have forced this change to accept any string as a harness
name and then reject it two phases later, at a point where the error can no longer name the manifest
line that caused it.

### `init` writes exactly one file, and its advice is only advice

`init` writes `harnaas.json` and nothing else: no harness directory, no `.harnaas/`, no `AGENTS.md`,
no `CLAUDE.md`, no ignore-file entry. Remaining setup is printed as guidance naming the command that
performs it, and there is deliberately no flag that makes `init` perform it.

The reason is ownership. A destination is managed only when the lockfile records it
([0001](../../../docs/adr/0001-ownership-lives-in-the-lockfile.md)), and `init` writes no lockfile —
so anything else it created would be *unmanaged*, and the very next `install` would report a conflict
against `init`'s own output. Entries in the ignore file have the same problem in reverse: `install`
maintains a managed block listing exactly the paths it installed, and an entry written before anything
is installed is a claim about files that do not exist. Keeping `init` to one file is what makes both
of those rules hold without special cases.

### Interactive is an affordance, never the only path

Every workflow is completable from a non-interactive terminal, and no information is reachable only
through a prompt, picker or full-screen interface. For `init` the form is a convenience over a
flag-driven path that is always available and is selected automatically when no terminal is attached.
This is not accessibility theatre: the primary consumers of these commands are CI jobs and coding
agents, neither of which has a terminal, and a workflow that only a human can complete is a workflow
CI cannot enforce.

Prompts render through an accessible-mode wrapper rather than the form library directly, and colour
comes from the terminal's own base palette with body text left unstyled, so output stays legible on a
light background and inverts with the user's theme.

### Logging is structured, file-bound and free of user content

Diagnostics go to a log file through `log/slog`, never to the terminal, so they can never interleave
with user output or corrupt a `--json` document. The privacy rule is inherited verbatim and treated as
hard: identifiers, paths, durations, counts and outcomes may be logged; file contents, memory or prompt
text, captured output and credentials may not. For harnaas this is sharper than usual, because the
files it handles — a team's instructions and rules — are exactly the ones nobody expects to find copied
into a log they did not know existed.

### Static analysis encodes the architecture rules, and the message names the replacement

golangci-lint runs the standard set plus roughly fifty additional linters, and — copying the source
CLI's most transferable idea — `forbidigo` rules turn "you must go through the abstraction" into build
failures whose messages name the function to use instead. The working-directory ban and the ban on
cobra's `Print*` helpers (which write to stderr and would corrupt piped output) both start here.
`nolintlint` requires every suppression to name a specific linter and give a reason, so widening a rule
is visible in review. The import-boundary AST test that protects the adapter registry follows the same
pattern and lands with `add-harnaas-install`, alongside the registry it protects.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- **Importing an architecture from a much larger CLI risks over-building.** harnaas has three commands;
  the source has dozens. Mitigated by importing the conventions and explicitly declining the subsystems
  — telemetry, auth, plugins, self-update — that only pay off at that scale.
- **A flat command package grows badly if the CLI does.** Accepted deliberately: the source CLI runs
  this convention past a hundred files, and the extraction trigger (an import cycle) is objective
  rather than a matter of taste.
- **Path-inferred type and id fails for a source that does not follow the convention.** The object form
  is the escape hatch, but a source laid out differently needs an object per asset, and the manifest
  loses the brevity that motivated inference. Accepted because the convention is the ecosystem's, and
  because the failure is a message naming the fix rather than a wrong install.
- **Strict decoding rejects a manifest written by a newer harnaas.** That is the intended trade for
  catching typos, and it is bounded by the version field: the failure is an explicit "upgrade harnaas"
  message rather than a confusing unknown-field error.
- **The root-only rule is unfriendly to monorepos**, where per-package harness assets are a plausible
  want. Accepted for v1: one declaration per repository is what makes the team-standardization story
  true, and relaxing it later is additive while tightening it later would not be.
- **The harness roster duplicates knowledge the adapters will own.** Mitigated by keeping it data-only
  and by the registry test in `add-harnaas-install` that fails if an adapter's id is missing from it,
  so the duplication cannot silently diverge.
- **`init`'s detection can be wrong in both directions** — a committed `.claude/` in a repository
  nobody uses Claude Code on, or a harness configured only in the user's home. Accepted because
  detection only pre-fills a selection the user confirms or overrides with a flag, and because the
  manifest states a guarantee rather than an observation.
- **Reserving exit code `2` diverges from the imported contract.** Contained by specifying it once in
  `cli-foundation`, giving it exactly one meaning, and stating the negative rule that no other command
  may use it.
- **There is no filesystem abstraction, so tests touch a real filesystem.** Accepted, following the
  source CLI, which uses temporary directories instead. Traversal safety comes from kernel-level
  directory confinement rather than from an interface seam, which is the stronger guarantee of the two.

## Open Questions

- **Does a `local` source key add anything over the `.harnaas/…` string form?** Both are accepted, and
  for the common case the path form is plainly better. The keyed form is kept because it lets a future
  source kind slot into one grammar rather than growing a second one; if it earns nothing by the time
  `install` ships, it should be removed while there is still no released behaviour to keep.
- **Should `harnaas.json` support a per-package manifest in a monorepo?** Deferred with the root-only
  rule above. Any answer must say what happens when two packages declare the same asset id.
- **Should a `rule` be expressible as inline content in the manifest** rather than always pointing at a
  file? Deferred: the file-pointer form is sufficient for v1, and inline content would complicate the
  digest model `lint` depends on.
- **Should harnaas publish a JSON Schema for `harnaas.json`** so editors can complete and validate it?
  Attractive given strict decoding, but validation lives in code today and a schema would be a second
  source of truth to keep in step. Deferred until the format has stopped moving.

Section 6 of the change is complete: `cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest` decodes and discovers `harnaas.json`, with fmt, lint and the full test suite clean (187 tests).

**What landed**

- **Document types** (`manifest.go`) — `Document` and `AssetEntry` hold the manifest field for field, uninterpreted. `Targets` distinguishes nil (undeclared, inherits `harnesses`) from an empty non-nil slice (declared empty, a violation section 7 must report), and `ObjectForm` records which form the author wrote so a remedy can direct them to the object form only if they aren't already there.
- **Two-pass decoding** (`decode.go`) — `version` is read on its own, leniently, *before* the strict pass. A manifest from a newer harnaas carries fields this binary doesn't know, and strictness would report the first of them as a misspelling; read first, it gets the one message that helps. Reading it with `json.Unmarshal` also rejects trailing data that a streaming decoder would drop in silence. Asset entries decode from `json.RawMessage` with the index in hand, because encoding/json attaches no array index to its errors and an entry has no other name at decode time.
- **Discovery** (`discover.go`) — `Load(ctx)` resolves the root from the context, scans for a stray manifest *before* the missing-manifest check, then reads. The scan skips dot-directories and dependency trees: a `harnaas.json` inside a vendored library is that library's, and failing the parent repo over it would name a file its author cannot edit.
- **Read-only by construction** — the only filesystem call is `os.ReadFile`, and an AST test over non-test sources fails on any write call or a `jsonutil` import.
- **Diagnostics** — one `*DecodeError` carrying `file:line:column`, a one-line problem and an edit; plus `*NotFoundError` (names `harnaas init`) and `*SubdirectoryError`. A table test asserts the problem-then-fix shape across all ten failure modes and that no remedy offers a fix command.

**One config change**: `.golangci.yaml` gained `wrapcheck.extra-ignore-sigs: [.ProjectRoot(]` — `paths.ProjectRoot`'s error is already a finished user-facing diagnostic, so wrapping it would prefix a complete message with plumbing. Every future command hits this, so it's configured once rather than suppressed per call site.

Section 7 (interpretation and validation) is next and consumes exactly these types.

input.summary: Added the manifest document, strict decoding and root-only discovery package (Section 6, tasks 6.1–6.8), taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 32/74 to 40/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
key_changes_made: cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest declares the decoded document — integer version, harnesses, sources map and an assets array whose entries keep their array index and their written form — with every field uninterpreted: an empty field means 'not declared', never 'declared as the default', which is the distinction the interpretation layer needs to default targets and scope

Version is read on its own, leniently, ahead of the strict pass, so a manifest written by a newer harnaas is refused with an upgrade message instead of a complaint about the first field this binary happens not to know; reading it with json.Unmarshal rather than a streaming decoder also rejects trailing data that would otherwise be dropped in silence

Strict decoding rejects unknown fields at both the document and asset-object level, malformed JSON with a file:line:column naming the parse position, and wrongly shaped fields named in the author's vocabulary rather than Go's — via a field-to-shape table, because reflection would print []string and map[string]string at a person reading JSON

Asset entries decode from json.RawMessage with the index in hand, accepting the string and object forms chosen from the first non-space byte and rejecting every other JSON type; encoding/json attaches no array index to its errors and an entry has no other name until its id is inferred
Every decode failure returns a nil document, so a partially decoded manifest can never reach a later phase and install a subset of what the project declared while reporting success
manifest.Load resolves the manifest from the context-carried project root, and manifest.Path is the single place the file's location is assembled so init and install cannot disagree about where it is

The search for a harnaas.json below the root runs before the missing-manifest check and skips dot-directories plus node_modules and vendor: a vendored library's manifest is its own, and a project whose only manifest sits in a subdirectory is never told to run `harnaas init`

Three diagnostics: *DecodeError carrying location, a one-line problem and an edit; *NotFoundError naming `harnaas init`; and *SubdirectoryError naming the file that will never be read and the one harnaas does read

Test coverage for section 6.8 plus a table asserting the problem-then-fix shape across all ten failure modes, that no remedy offers a fix command, and an AST guardrail over non-test sources asserting no write call and no jsonutil import has crept into the read-only loader

CLAUDE.md records the two new load-bearing decisions — the version pre-pass and the root-only rule with its dependency-directory skips — and .golangci.yaml exempts paths.ProjectRoot from wrapcheck, because its error is already a finished user-facing diagnostic that a caller would only prefix with plumbing
key_learnings: json.Unmarshal validates the whole input and rejects a second top-level value, so a version pre-pass over the full document makes an explicit trailing-data check unreachable — the check was written, proved dead, and removed in favour of documenting that the pre-pass settles it.

encoding/json reports an unknown field as a bare fmt.Errorf, not a typed error, so recognising it means matching the literal prefix `json: unknown field ` and unquoting the rest; the translation falls through to reporting the raw message if that wording ever changes, which is worse but never wrong.

An asset entry decoded from its own json.RawMessage carries offsets relative to the entry, so any line:column derived from them names the wrong line in the file. Scoping the locator to an entry and having it refuse to report a location at all is the fix — one comment in one place rather than a mutation at each call site.

wrapcheck fires on errors returned from any other package including same-module ones, which will hit every future command calling paths.ProjectRoot. Configuring extra-ignore-sigs once is the right answer where the callee's error is already a complete problem-then-fix diagnostic; wrapping it would prefix a finished message with the caller's plumbing.

The `exhaustive` linter's default (default-signifies-exhaustive: false) makes a switch on reflect.Kind a lint failure even with a default clause, which is a practical reason to describe expected JSON shapes from a field-name table rather than by reflection — and the table produces better messages anyway.

Section 7's interpretation layer is now fully unblocked: it reads Document/AssetEntry, and the two decode-time distinctions it depends on are already pinned by tests — nil vs empty Targets, and empty-string overrides meaning undeclared.
